# How to practice for a job interview with an AI mock interviewer tonight

> **In short:** You can run a realistic mock interview with any major AI assistant tonight by giving it the job description, asking it to play interviewer, and stress-testing one tough answer at a time. It won't replace a real human, but it will sharpen what you actually say.

Job interviews don't reward memorization — they reward clarity under pressure. Tonight you can build that clarity with a practice partner that already lives in your phone or browser: an AI assistant. The trick isn't to ask random questions. It's to run a short, repeatable session that stress-tests your real answers before a human ever hears them. Below is a method you can use tonight, and again the night before any interview.

## Before you start
- An account with any major AI assistant — **ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, and Le Chat** all work for this. Use whichever you already have; don't sign up for a new one tonight.
- The job description for the role. Copy-paste the whole posting, even if it's long — the AI uses every line.
- A quiet 30–45 minutes, ideally with headphones and a microphone so you can hear yourself.
- Optional: a notes app open on your phone so you can save weak spots at the end.

## Step 1 — Open a fresh chat with your AI assistant
Open the AI assistant of your choice in a browser or app and start a brand-new conversation. What you'll see is a blank chat box — no prior context, no leftover questions from yesterday. This matters because the assistant draws on the whole chat thread when it replies, so a clean slate means a clean practice session. In ChatGPT, look for a top-left button that says **New chat**; in Claude, Gemini, and Copilot, look for **New chat** or a **+** icon near the conversation list. On mobile, you may need to swipe to your conversation history first before the button appears.
💬 Example: just open the chat — no typing yet.
You'll know it worked when you see an empty message box with a placeholder like "Message…" or "Ask anything."

## Step 2 — Tell the AI exactly what role you're practicing for
Paste the job description into the chat, then add two or three lines about your background. What you'll see is a long message appear, followed by the assistant's reply — usually a short acknowledgment like "Got it, here's how I'll approach this." The assistant now has the context it needs to ask realistic questions instead of generic ones. If your tool has a **Custom instructions** or **Memory** setting, you can paste the role there so it persists across chats; otherwise just paste it into the first message of this session. On Claude and ChatGPT those settings live under your profile picture; on Gemini they're under **Settings**.
💬 Example: "I'm preparing for a Senior Customer Success interview at a B2B SaaS company. Here is the job description: [paste]. My background: 4 years in support, promoted once, led a small team. Please ask me one question at a time, like a real interviewer would."
You'll know it worked when the assistant references your actual role or company in its next reply — not a generic "tell me about yourself."

## Step 3 — Start with the one question you find hardest
Ask the assistant to ask you the single question you're most worried about — usually a behavioral or scenario question, not the opener. What you'll see is the assistant posing it the way a real interviewer would: *"Tell me about a time you dealt with a difficult customer."* Read the question, then **answer out loud** — even if you're typing, speak the answer aloud so you catch filler words, awkward pauses, and rambling. This is the most underused part of practice, and the part that actually changes how you sound in the room. If your assistant has a voice mode (ChatGPT and Gemini both do on desktop and mobile), switch to it now; otherwise read your typed answer out loud to yourself once you're done.
💬 Example: "Ask me one question at a time. Start with: 'Tell me about a time you had to win back an unhappy customer.'"
You'll know it worked when you've actually spoken a full answer of roughly 60–90 seconds — not just thought one.

## Step 4 — Ask for specific, structured feedback
Once you've answered, prompt the assistant to score your reply and point to one improvement. What you'll see is a short rubric — usually a 1-to-5 rating on clarity, specificity, or impact, plus one thing to tighten. This is where generic praise is useless, so ask for criticism directly; the assistant now becomes a coach instead of a yes-machine. If it forgets and just says "great answer!", tell it again to be tougher — most assistants default to polite, especially in voice mode. On the free plan of all the assistants listed above, text feedback is unlimited; voice mode may have a small daily cap.
💬 Example: "Rate my answer from 1 to 5 on clarity, specificity, and impact. Give me one strength and one specific thing to improve. Be honest — I'd rather hear it from you than from an interviewer."
You'll know it worked when you can name one concrete sentence or word you'd change before tomorrow.

## Step 5 — Run a five-question dress rehearsal
Once your warm-up answer feels solid, ask the assistant to run a full short interview. What you'll see is it moving through five questions in sequence — one at a time, waiting for your reply before continuing. Treat this like the real thing: no peeking at notes, no redoing an answer, and try to keep each answer between 60 and 90 seconds. If your assistant has voice mode, use it for this round; speaking back-to-back is closer to the actual interview than typing. Set a phone timer for 10 minutes so you don't run over. If the screen shows a **Stop** or **Regenerate** button, ignore both and just answer naturally.
💬 Example: "Now run a 5-question mock interview, one question at a time. Wait for my answer before moving on. Mix behavioral and role-specific questions."
You'll know it worked when you've answered five questions back-to-back out loud and feel a bit tired — that's the real interview muscle kicking in.

## Step 6 — Capture your three weakest spots before you close the chat
End the session by asking the assistant to summarize the patterns it noticed — vague answers, missing numbers, weak openings. What you'll see is a short list of two to four patterns, plus the specific questions that exposed them. Screenshot it or copy it into your notes app before you close the chat, because tomorrow you'll want to practice those exact spots. This single summary is what turns a random practice session into a repeatable method: each night you run the same drill, you knock down one more weak pattern. Be aware — the assistant may flatter you here too, so push for the harshest pattern if its list feels too soft.
💬 Example: "Based on this whole session, list the three patterns that hurt my answers most, and the one question I should drill tomorrow."
You'll know it worked when you have a 3-item checklist saved somewhere outside the chat.

## Common mistakes
- **Reading your answer instead of saying it.** Typing an answer and reading it back to yourself feels safe but doesn't catch the rambling, filler words, or long pauses a real interviewer hears. Speak every answer out loud, even if it feels awkward.
- **Letting the assistant be too polite.** Most AI assistants default to "great answer!" — which is useless for practice. If your feedback feels like a hug, tell the assistant directly to score you from 1 to 5 and give one specific improvement.
- **Practicing only "tell me about yourself."** That opener is rarely the question that decides the interview. Spend at least half your session on the two or three harder behavioral and scenario questions for the actual role — that's where the real anxiety hides.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** If you're between jobs or thinking about a change, this same loop works for promotion conversations, salary reviews, or even asking a landlord to fix something — anywhere a clear, structured answer matters more than a clever one.
- **For your business or work:** Use this method to rehearse client pitches, performance reviews, or tough conversations with a colleague. The "AI asks, you answer out loud, get one specific critique" pattern generalizes to almost any high-stakes talk.
- **If you're just getting started:** Don't try to do all six steps tonight. Do Step 1, paste the job description, and answer one tough question out loud. That's already more practice than most candidates do.

## Try it now
Open your AI assistant right now, paste the job description into a fresh chat, and type: *"Ask me one question at a time. Start with the hardest behavioral question for a [role] interview."* Then answer it out loud. That's the whole loop in two minutes — and the easiest way to find out where you actually stand tonight.
